title: The Atlantic jigsaw
hook: South America and Africa look like they fit. Close the ocean and test it.

knows: that South America and Africa have matching-looking coasts
doesNotKnow: that the match holds up as geometry when one continent is turned as a rigid piece

misconception: The coast match is a coincidence people over-read; continents have always been where they are.
objective: The learner can describe that turning South America as one rigid piece about a single pole closes it against Africa, with Brazil's bulge in the Gulf of Guinea, and that this fit is evidence the continents were joined.

claims.text: On the stage, South America is turned as one solid piece 57° about a single point in the North Atlantic (44°N, 30.6°W), marked by a 'pivot just above (44°N)' arrow at the top edge of the view (the point itself projects just above the frame); the red dot's trail is an arc around that point, the slider and 'Turned' readout show the angle in degrees, and the coast closes against Africa's.
claims.source: Bullard, E., Everett, J. E. and Smith, A. G. (1965), The fit of the continents around the Atlantic, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 258(1088): 41-51 (South America to Africa: pole 44.0 N, 30.6 W, rotation 57.0 degrees, fitted at the 500-fathom isobath). Parameters from the brief and builder recall; not opened (network blocked). It is a best fit of margins, not a plate-motion history. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): RE-OPENED in pass 9: this was marked verified but its source says the parameters came from builder recall and the paper was not opened. Bullard, Everett and Smith (1965), Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 258: 41-51, is unreachable (royalsocietypublishing.org 403); a web search found no secondary source quoting 44.0 N, 30.6 W, 57.0 degrees. Needs a human source check of the paper's table. Note: c4 (500-fathom contour) rests on the same unopened paper. | v2 (2026-10-14): claim text rewritten to match the revised stage; previous verification void, needs re-check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Pass 21: still not opened (royalsocietypublishing, geologie.ens.fr OCR copy and Morgan 1968 PDF all blocked to fetch). Web-search extracts: an OCR of the paper lists fit 9 (500 fm) as '44.0 30.6 57.0', and Morgan (1968) cites Bullard et al. for a 44.0 N, 30.6 W pole; but Virtual Explorer (2007) lists Bullard et al. (1965) as 42.9, -30.1, 57.1 and gives 44/-30.6/57 to Smith and Hallam (1970). The learner sentence depends on the unopened table and secondary sources conflict, so disputed. To clear: a human opens Table 1 (fit 9) in Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 258: 41-51 (copy at geologie.ens.fr/50years_plate_tectonics/phil-trans-r-soc-lond-a.pdf). · Fact-check pass 23 2026-10-14: Still disputed, unchanged since pass 21 (claim and stage not edited). The source host (geologie.ens.fr) does not resolve from this sandbox, so Table 1 of Bullard, Everett and Smith (1965) is still unopened. To clear: a human opens Table 1, fit 9. | REVISED v3 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): v3 drops the attribution 'which is the fit Bullard, Everett and Smith published in 1965', because Table 1 of that paper could not be opened and secondary sources disagree on the pole (44.0/30.6/57.0 vs 42.9/30.1/57.1). The sentence now says only what the stage does: the angle and the pole are the lesson's model parameters (Demo.tsx POLE, ANGLE), and the closing is the stage check behind c2 and c3. The learner no longer sees the paper or a claim that these are published values. Unverified. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 24): VERIFIED. Describes the stage only: POLE [-30.6, 44] (lon, lat), ANGLE 57 in Demo.tsx; 44°N 30.6°W is open North Atlantic. Own node Rodrigues rotation + countries-110m: bulge (34.8 W, 7.1 S) -> 7.27 E, 4.98 N, 61 km from an African vertex (2,928 km before); Brazil east-coast vertices (25) end mean 128 km, max 199 km from the West/South African coast. No longer attributes the parameters to Bullard et al. | Builder revision v5 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, wave G r7): pivot = projection(POLE), at y ≈ -6 in this view, so an arrow at the top edge points to it (a '+' is drawn instead if it is inside the frame); trail = projection(rotation(POLE, 57·k/100)(TIP)) for k = 0, 2, ... up to the slider, plus the current point; slider format and 'Turned' readout = round(57 × pct / 100)°. The trail points rotation(POLE, 57k/100)(TIP) stay 51.241 deg from the pole at every k, so the trail is an arc of a circle about the pivot. deg(pct) = round(57*pct/100): slider format and Turned readout show 0..57 deg. Bulge ends at 7.27 E, 4.98 N (pass 24 fit check unchanged: POLE, ANGLE, TIP, outlines not edited). claims.text: Brazil's eastern bulge lands in the Gulf of Guinea, near Nigeria and Cameroon.
claims.source: Rodrigues rotation of (34.8 W, 7.1 S) by +57 degrees about (44 N, 30.6 W) gives 7.27 E, 4.98 N; the nearest 1:110m African outline vertex is Nigeria's, 61 km away (artifacts/scratch/w1-jigsaw.mjs). The rotation sense (+57) is the one that brings South America to Africa; -57 sends it to the Pacific. | v6 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): learner r8 (90-word budget): reveal now "It tucks into the Gulf of Guinea, near Nigeria and Cameroon." ('under West Africa's coast' cut); the Gulf of Guinea label moved up-left of its dot, clear of the red dot. Needs re-check.

claims.text: With today's coarse coastlines the fit is rough.
claims.source: 1,551 one-degree sample points inside the South American shapes: 3 land inside an African country after the turn; Brazil's east-coast vertices end a mean 148 km (max 302 km) from the nearest African vertex (w1-jigsaw.mjs). No km figure is shown to the learner. | v6 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): learner r8: the reveal sentence "Its coast closed against Africa's with small gaps and overlaps" was cut (told; nothing on the stage marks gaps or overlaps), so the 'small gaps and overlaps' half of this claim is withdrawn. What remains is the reveal's "The fit here is rough: these outlines are coarse." Text reworded; needs re-check.

claims.text: A rotation on the sphere keeps South America's size and shape; only its place changes.
claims.source: Rotations of the sphere are isometries. Demo.tsx applies one rotation to every vertex (kit mapFeature).

claims.text: The South Atlantic began opening roughly 130 million years ago.
claims.source: Frisch, Meschede and Blakey (2011), Plate Tectonics, Springer: South Atlantic rifting and opening in the Early Cretaceous, about 140-120 Ma. Not opened by the builder. | v2: sentence no longer shown to learners; withdrawn.

claims.text: Two coasts this far apart rarely match by chance; the fit is evidence the continents were once joined.
claims.source: Interpretive claim; Bullard et al. (1965) and standard plate-tectonics texts present the fit as evidence for continental drift. The lesson does not claim the fit alone proves it.

claims.text: A 'Size on the globe' readout shows South America's area on the sphere, 17.9 million km² for these 1:110m outlines, and it stays the same at every turn; the piece only looks bigger as it moves toward the middle because the globe view squashes shapes near its edge.
claims.source: Demo.tsx areaM(): d3 geoArea of the (rotated) FeatureCollection × R² (EARTH_RADIUS_KM 6371.0088), one decimal. Builder's node script (2026-10-14, d3-geo + countries-110m.json, the same 12 countries plus French Guiana): 17.886 million km² unrotated. Rotation about an axis maps great-circle edges to great-circle edges, so the spherical area is unchanged. Orthographic foreshortening: scale along the radial direction falls as cos of the angular distance from the view centre (Snyder 1987, Map Projections: A Working Manual, USGS PP 1395, orthographic). Builder statement, not self-verified. | FC pass 26 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Same script: geoArea x R^2 (R 6371.0088) of the 12 countries + French Guiana = 17.886 million km^2, '17.9' at every integer slider value 0..100 (min = max to float precision), as a rotation must give. Squash: orthographic radial scale = cos c (rho = R sin c, d rho/dc = R cos c; tangential scale 1), so drawn area scales by cos c; the piece centroid moves from 41.7 deg to 12.1 deg off the view centre, predicted ratio cos12.1/cos41.7 = 1.31, measured projected path area 9,264 -> 12,128 px^2 (x1.31). Re-derived, not resting on the unopened Snyder text. | v6 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): learner r8: reveal sentence now "It looked bigger near the middle of the globe, but its size stayed 17.9 million km² throughout."; the legend line ('The globe squashes shapes near its edge.') shows during explore and is hidden at the reveal for the phone fit; the Size on the globe readout stays on screen. Needs re-check.

recall.question: When South America is turned back against Africa, Brazil's eastern bulge sits:
options: In the Gulf of Guinea, under West Africa
recall.why: Turned as one rigid piece about a single pole, the bulge tucks under West Africa's coast into the Gulf of Guinea.
